newsitem.title: UK: U.S. firms to buy Britain's Yorkshire for $2.4 billion.
newsitem.headline: U.S. firms to buy Britain's Yorkshire for $2.4 billion.

text.p: Ohio-based American Electric Power Co. Inc. and Public Service Co. of Colorado said Monday they would buy Britain's Yorkshire Electricity Group Plc for 1.5 billion pounds ($2.43 billion).

The two U.S. utilities said they expected the acquisition of one of Britain's last independent regional electricity companies to create new opportunities in power supply, technology and power generation.
If approved, the British utility would be bought by Yorkshire Holdings, a firm owned equally by the two U.S. companies, they said.

The deal, which would be the seventh acquisition of a British utility by an American company, leaves Southern Electric Plc as Britain's only remaining independent regional electricity company of the 12 that were privatised in 1990.
"Yorkshire is particularly attractive to us because of its tradition of low-cost, high-customer service," American Electric Chairman Linn Draper told reporters in a telephone conference call.
Yorkshire said it would not contest the bid as it saw no competitive advantage to staying independent.

"We always said that if somebody came along and offered us a sufficiently high price, and a good deal for our shareholders, we would consider it. And we think this is a very fair price," Yorkshire Chairman Christopher Hampson said.
American Electric, based in Columbus, Ohio, and Denver-based Public Service of Colorado said they expected to receive British regulatory clearance before the end of May.
Draper said he did not expect regulatory roadblocks, but some British analysts said if the Labour Party wins a May 22 national election, it could be less amenable to the deal.

The ruling Conservative Party government already has nodded through bids for 10 of the 12 regional electricity companies. But Labour, ahead in current opinion polls, has proposed a windfall tax on utilities and criticised so-called "fat-cat" pay awards for senior management of the companies.

"Financially, for shareholders, it looks a fair offer," said SocGen analyst Marshall Whiting. "(But) not everybody thinks it's going to go through ... That's what the (share) price is saying to us," he added.
After the announcement, Yorkshire's shares rose but remained below the offer price of about 927 pence ($15.03).
The U.S. utilities said they expected the deal to immediately add to their earnings and that they did not foresee restructuring charges from the transaction.
They also said they would reap unspecified cost savings from the deal, noting Yorkshire management would be retained. But they stopped short of pledging not to cut Yorkshire's work force.
The U.S. companies said they expected to expand Yorkshire's generation of electricity and to benefit from its experience when Britain opens up the electricity supply market in 1998.
The U.S. companies said they had considered other possible acquisitions in Britain and elsewhere.
Some U.S. analysts thought the partnership structure left the door open for further acquisitions by American Electric.
Smith Barney analyst William Tilles said the Ohio company had the resources to consummate a deal like this by itself, so another, possibly larger transaction could also occur.
Wheat First Butcher Singer analyst Thomas Hamlin agreed.
"Yes, it frees up some equity for AEP to do some other foreign deals," Hamlin said.

David Schanzer, a Janney Montgomery Scott analyst, said U.S. companies, facing coming deregulation at home, are wise to gain experience in a less regulated, more competitive environment such as Britain's.
"The better companies in the United States tend to recognise the opportunities overseas," Schanzer said.
Analysts said the deal seemed positive for the U.S. firms.
Legg Mason Wood Walker analyst Ronald Tanner said, "We don't get real excited about these (British) acquisitions but in general they do well... It's not like hitting a home run but it's a single."
Yorkshire owns a 22.5 percent stake in a British telecommunications firm, Ionica. In October, AEP formed a new subsidiary called AEP Communications.
Some power companies are exploring telecommunications options such as incorporating fiber optic lines on existing property rights of way.
A Public Service-Colorado merger with Southwestern Public Service Co. is pending.
Public Service of Colorado's stock rose $1 to $39.875 while American Electric stock rose 25 cents to $42.125, both on the New York Stock Exchange.
